cases.name: Technective
cases.text: Use your own Technective pre-release booklet for this case: the set task brief, the UK smartwatch market, the competitor profiles, the primary research report and the media options. This site doesn't copy the booklet, so have it open next to you and quote its facts and figures in your answers.

terms.d: Objectives that are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound
A broad, long-term goal that a business wants to achieve
A specific, measurable target that helps a business achieve its aim
A planned set of marketing activities, over a set time, to achieve specific objectives
The specific group of customers a business aims its product and marketing at
Dividing a market into groups of customers with similar needs or characteristics
Grouping customers by factors such as age, gender, income or occupation
Grouping customers by their lifestyle, values, interests and attitudes
Grouping customers by where they live, e.g. region, country, town or city
The total number of customers, or the total value of sales, in a market
The percentage of total sales in a market made by one business or brand
How a market is made up, e.g. how many businesses compete in it and how big they are
When a market has so many similar products that there is little room left for growth
The general direction a market is moving in over time, e.g. growing demand for a feature
New information collected first-hand by a business for its own purpose, e.g. a questionnaire
Information that already exists because someone else collected it, e.g. reports and statistics
Numerical information that can be counted and analysed, e.g. percentages
Information about opinions, feelings and reasons, usually given in words
The number of people who take part in a piece of research
How far research results can be trusted to be accurate and to give the same results again
A feature that makes a product different from, and better than, its competitors' products
Something that lets a business do better than its rivals, e.g. lower costs or a stronger brand
When customers keep buying from the same brand instead of switching to competitors
Another business selling similar products to the same customers
The combination of product, price, place and promotion used to market a product
Setting a high price to reflect high quality, status or exclusivity
Setting a low price at launch to attract customers and win market share quickly
Cutting prices for a short time, e.g. discounts or offers, to boost sales
When competitors keep cutting their prices to win customers from each other
Encouraging customers to buy a more expensive version or extra products
The full range of products that a business sells
A review of a business's internal strengths and weaknesses, and external opportunities and threats
A review of the political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors outside a business
A factor outside the business's control that affects it, e.g. the economy or new laws
Paying to support an event, team or person in return for promoting the brand
Working with people who have large social media followings to promote a product
Paying for an online advert each time someone clicks on it
The number of people who pass or visit a particular place, e.g. a shop or billboard
The channels used to send a marketing message, e.g. TV, social media, magazines or billboards
The amount of money set aside to spend on a marketing campaign
Identifying, anticipating and satisfying customer needs profitably
Anticipate, recognise, stimulate and satisfy demand
A small, specific segment of a larger market, e.g. left-handed scissors
Aiming a product at all or most of the market, e.g. shampoo, promoted through mass media
Grouping customers by how they behave towards products, e.g. usage rate or brand loyalty
The image a brand gives off to customers, which has a lasting impact on the business
Using a unique name, logo, colours or slogan to identify a product and set it apart from competitors
A factor inside the business that affects a campaign, e.g. cost, finance or staff expertise
Whether research is relevant to the business and measures what it should
When research isn't conducted fairly, e.g. the sample doesn't represent the market
Existing data from inside the business, e.g. sales records or loyalty card data
Free official data about the population, e.g. age, unemployment and households
A magazine for one industry with news, statistics and trends
Examining information in detail to understand patterns, relationships, causes or implications
The stages a product goes through: introduction, growth, maturity, decline
Changing a product or its marketing to give it fresh appeal and delay decline
Setting a high launch price, then lowering it as competitors arrive
Adding a profit margin to the cost of making the product
Setting prices in line with competitors
Making a product different from rivals' products, e.g. by quality, design or packaging
Form is how a product looks; function is what it does
Managing a business's reputation and goodwill by giving information
Low-cost, unconventional advertising in an unexpected place
Paying for a product to appear in TV programmes or films
Face-to-face or telephone selling by trained staff
Selling straight from the manufacturer to the customer

steps.title: Find the aim of the business
steps.intro: Find what Technective wants to achieve by launching the smartwatch. Every later step links back to this aim.

fields.label: The aim
fields.hint: In one sentence: what does Technective want to achieve? Look at the set task brief and the section on taking advantage of the smartwatch market.

fields.label: Where you found it

The aim comes from the booklet, not made up
Says where in the booklet the aim comes from
steps.tip: Keep the aim broad (what they want overall). The SMART objectives in step 2 are the specific targets.

checks: Three different objectives
Each is Specific: says exactly what will be achieved
Each is Measurable: includes a number or percentage

steps.tip: Check every objective against all five letters. A number and a deadline are the easiest marks to lose.

example.title: Your teacher's example (Knights of Cocoa, a different case study)
text: 1 objective that Knights of Cocoa could use is to create a new sugar-free chocolate bar within the next 6 months. This would help them to achieve the aim of increasing sales, because currently sugar-free chocolate is trending within the market and competitors are offering the same products. If KOC releases a sugar-free chocolate bar it is likely that customers will purchase this, which will in turn increase their sales.
1 objective that they could use is to advertise their website on Instagram, resulting in 10% more sales in 2 weeks.
Both objectives are linked to trends within the market.
example.note: To push for D*, make every objective fully SMART: the first example has a deadline but no number to measure it by.

text: Chocolate market is increasing each year – this will help KOC achieve the aim to increase their sales because there is a larger opportunity to influence new customers each year to purchase their product, increasing sales.

More people shopping online for chocolate – this will help them achieve the aim of increasing sales because KOC can use this to their advantage and invest more into their website and advertising their website to let people know that they sell online, which in turn should increase the traffic to their website, resulting in a higher amount of sales.

example.title: Your teacher's example (Knights of Cocoa, a different case study)
text: Hotel Chocolat is one of the largest competitors to KOC because they operate both online and have a high presence with retail locations. This could be an issue for KOC because they have been established since 2004, therefore they have a strong customer base and market presence, which could result in KOC not being able to increase their sales because it might be difficult to compete with such a large business.

Thorntons are currently closing all of their retail locations. This could positively impact KOC because it means Thorntons have reduced their presence on the high street. If KOC choose to open further retail stores or promote their current retail stores on social media, this could increase the number of customers within those stores, which could result in an increase in sales.
example.note: Notice one competitor is a threat and the other is an opportunity, and both end by linking to the aim.

steps.title: Market research: reliability, validity and bias
steps.intro: Judge Technective's primary research. Use figures from the research report for each part.

fields.label: Reliability
fields.hint: Can the results be trusted and repeated? Think about sample size and how it was collected.

fields.label: Validity
fields.hint: Does it measure what Technective needs? Think about who was asked, when, and the questions.

fields.label: Bias
fields.hint: Who is over- or under-represented? Compare the sample with the market.

fields.label: So what for Technective?
fields.hint: What does this mean for decisions about the aim?

checks: Reliability: judges whether the results can be trusted or repeated (e.g. sample size), with evidence
Validity: judges whether the research measures what Technective needs (e.g. who, when, which questions)
Bias: identifies who is over- or under-represented, with evidence
Uses figures from the research report
Says what this means for Technective's decisions
steps.tip: Don't just say 'it's unreliable'. Say why, give the figure, and say what that could lead Technective to get wrong.

example.title: Your teacher's example (Knights of Cocoa, a different case study)
text: Technological – Point: One technological factor which could impact KOC is the use of websites. Evidence: This is because 'Thorntons had a rapid increase in online sales'. Explain: If KOC sold on a website, similar to what Thorntons do, this would benefit them because they would be able to sell 24/7, which is likely to increase sales. With the increase in sales, they are likely to be more profitable because they won't have to pay a portion of the revenue to any supermarkets or third-party sellers. Link: However, if KOC only sell via website, this could also negatively affect their sales because a number of their competitors also sell products online, meaning that the online chocolate market is already heavily saturated, so their website could get lost and not receive any traffic.

Political – Point: One political factor that could impact KOC is the increased import and export fees. Evidence: This is because 'UK chocolate businesses now export to over 149 different countries'. Explain: This could impact KOC because it is now becoming more expensive to export products due to leaving the EU. With UK chocolate businesses heavily exporting to a number of different countries, this will cause their expenditure to increase. Link: This could stop KOC from achieving the aim of increasing sales because KOC will need to increase their prices to absorb the additional export costs. This leads to customers finding a cheaper alternative to purchase their chocolate from, which would decrease their sales.

learn.title: Unit 2: Developing a Marketing Campaign (Learning Aims A, B and C)

sections.heading: How you're assessed
sections.text: Unit 2 is a set task. You get 2 hours of preparation time the day before the exam to analyse the case study data and make 2 pages of notes to take in. The notes can't contain analysis, or they'll be taken away. Then you have a 3-hour exam, typed on a computer, where you create a marketing campaign for the business in the case study.
points: The exam is worth 70 marks
Grade boundaries: Distinction 54, Merit 39, Pass 25, Near Pass 12

Topics covered: the role of marketing, aims and objectives, types of market, segmentation, branding, internal and external influences, how market research is used, types of research, validity and reliability, analysis tools, the marketing mix and marketing campaigns

sections.heading: What is marketing?
sections.text: Marketing is the process of identifying, anticipating and satisfying customer needs profitably.
points: Example: a t-shirt brand uses Instagram ads and influencer partnerships to promote a new eco-friendly clothing line
Marketing helps a business attract customers, build brand awareness and increase sales by promoting the right product to the right people at the right time
The 4 key purposes of marketing: anticipate demand → recognise demand → stimulate demand → satisfy demand

diagram.alt: The four key purposes of marketing as a chain of four steps: anticipate demand (work out what customers will want), recognise demand (spot what they want now), stimulate demand (make them want it through promotion), satisfy demand (give them what they want so they come back).
diagram.caption: Anticipate, recognise, stimulate, satisfy.

sections.heading: Aims and objectives
sections.text: An aim is a purpose or intention: the desired outcome. For a business it is the bigger picture, the main thing it wants to achieve. It is long term, achieved over a long period of time.
points: Example aim: "We want to be the market leader for skateboard sales in the UK"
Objectives break the aim down into smaller tasks. They are short term and easier to achieve
Objectives can be changed once they have been achieved, but they always support the aim
Example: aim = market leader for skateboards; objectives = increase sales, attract new customers, build brand awareness
Aims and objectives can differ for niche and mass markets, e.g. a 30% rise in brand awareness may suit a small niche, but a mass market might target 10% because the market is so much bigger

sections.heading: SMART objectives
sections.text: To get the marks in your exam, your objectives need to be SMART.

head: Letter
Means
Example (Jordan 1s)
rows: Who, what, where, when. Define the goal as much as possible
Increase sales of Jordan 1s (not just 'increase sales')
How will you track progress and know the goal is accomplished?
Is the goal reasonable enough to be accomplished, not out of reach?
30% is achievable for Nike; 1000% every 2 months isn't
Can the team achieve it with the resources they have? Is it relevant to the business, the case study and the main aim?
Important in your exam: link it to the case study
Give it a deadline, which helps make it measurable and achievable

points: Worked example (Decreal Gear): aim = increase revenue. Objective: gain 10,000 followers on Instagram within one month. If they achieve this, 10,000 more people are aware of Decreal Gear, and some of these followers could become customers, increasing revenue
Not SMART: "To get more customers" (no number or deadline). "Improve customer satisfaction by 100% in 1 week" isn't achievable or realistic
SMART: "Increase sales revenue by 10% each month, for 12 months"

sections.heading: Niche and mass markets
sections.text: A market is a place where buyers and sellers meet. It can be physical or non-physical. A business decides whether to aim its product at a particular segment (a niche market) or appeal to the whole market (the mass market).

head: Niche market: advantages
Niche market: disadvantages
rows: A firm can adapt its products to meet the specific needs of the niche market
Can limit high profit because there are fewer customers
Easier to target customers and use specific promotion aimed at smaller groups
Growth of the market can bring larger competitors into it
Can be a limited size market

points: Niche marketing targets a product at a small segment of a larger market, e.g. Rolex watches, left-handed scissors. Niches appear when a business spots needs not met by other firms

Mass marketing aims a product at all (or most) of the market, e.g. shampoo, ketchup. It's an unsegmented market, sold through mass retailers and promoted through mass media such as TV and the internet
Summary: niche marketing is generally used by smaller businesses with a smaller customer base; mass marketing by larger businesses with the resources to market to everyone

sections.heading: Market segmentation
sections.text: Market segmentation is dividing a large group of potential customers into smaller groups (segments) based on shared characteristics, so a business can target its products and campaigns more effectively.

head: Type
Groups customers by
Examples
rows: Age, family size, occupation, social class, income, religion, gender, education, nationality, ethnicity
How they actually behave towards products
User status, occasions, usage rates, brand loyalty, benefits sought, readiness to buy
Lifestyle, values, personality, interests, attitudes, opinions

points: Why businesses segment: spot gaps, target particular groups, sell more products, waste fewer resources, offer a wider range of differentiated products, create customer loyalty, benefit from economies of scale
In a campaign it helps choose the right audience (e.g. 16–18-year-olds who love fashion), design messages that appeal to them, and pick the best places to advertise (e.g. TikTok, Instagram)
Example: Fresh & Kind (recipe boxes) could segment by dietary requirements, e.g. vegan, so it can specialise the meals it offers that segment

sections.heading: Branding, brand image and USPs
sections.text: Branding is how a business creates a unique image and identity, using a name, logo, colours, slogan and overall feel to identify a product and differentiate it from competitors (e.g. Nike's swoosh and "Just Do It").
points: Benefits of a strong brand: recognition, customer loyalty, word-of-mouth recommendations, higher demand, preferred over own-brand labels, higher prices can be charged, global recognition, new products can use the brand's strength, brand stretching to diversify
Brand image is the image the brand gives off to customers. It has a lasting impact, so a business must keep a positive brand image to keep returning and new customers
A USP (unique selling point) is a feature or benefit that separates a product from its competitors and helps gain market share, e.g. Amazon Prime's next-day delivery
USP advantages: customer satisfaction, repeat purchases and recommendations, lower marketing cost, higher loyalty, can charge higher prices, differentiation, competitive advantage, economies of scale
USP risks: wasted materials, financial costs (legal costs, compensation), loss of customers, bad reputation, reworking products, imitation/copying, substitutes

sections.heading: Influences on a marketing campaign
sections.text: Internal influences come from inside the business; external influences come from outside it.

head: Small business
Large business
rows: Less money to spend; less able to borrow; less likely to benefit from economies of scale
More able to raise finance; benefits from economies of scale; more disposable money
Less access to resources; may need more niche resources
More access to resources; more options to finance them

points: Internal influences: cost of the campaign, availability of finance, expertise of staff, size and culture of the business
External influences: social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal, ethical

sections.heading: Why businesses do market research
sections.text: Market research is collecting information about customers, competitors and the market to make better decisions. It helps a business identify gaps in the market and business opportunities.
points: 1) Identify the target market. Research must be based on the target market: asking the wrong people wastes time and money, gives feedback that doesn't reflect the target audience, and can lead to unsuitable products

2) Identify the size, structure and trends of the market. Size helps plan the budget (and whether to aim at a mass or niche market); structure links to demographics and the research methods to use; trends show what customers want, where and when they'll buy
3) Identify the competition: what competitors sell, their promotions, and the threats they pose, so marketing can influence buying behaviour more effectively
Research helps choose product features (flavour, size, price), the right audience and the best advertising methods, e.g. a milkshake brand asking teenagers which flavours they like

sections.heading: Primary research
sections.text: Primary research is first-hand information collected by the business for a specific purpose.
points: Why do it: it's personalised (questions tailored to the topic and target audience) and gives more in-depth, accurate information for decisions such as what to produce, where to sell and what to charge
Why not: it typically costs more and takes longer than secondary research
Quantitative data: numbers and statistics, e.g. '80% of participants agree'; used to predict trends
Qualitative data: written answers and opinions from fewer people, giving in-depth explanations

sections.heading: Secondary research
sections.text: Secondary (desk) research uses data that already exists, collected by someone else for a different purpose, e.g. government reports, industry publications, websites and previous surveys.

head: Source
What it is
rows: Sales records from the business's own database, broken down by dates, times and products, used to spot patterns and trends
Detailed data on each customer (e.g. Tesco Clubcard) for personalised offers
Reports on markets and the economy, e.g. Mintel; often paid for
Free data on the population, e.g. age and gender split, unemployment, households
Magazines for a specific industry with news, statistics and trends
TV, newspapers, radio, magazines, the internet and social media

points: Why use it: cheaper (no need to pay for research) and saves time
Why not: it may not be fully relevant (it was done for another business) and may be outdated, leading to wrong decisions
Businesses use it to make future decisions, spot trends and see what competitors are doing

sections.heading: Validity, reliability and bias
sections.text: Validity: is the information relevant to the business (does it measure what it should)? Reliability: can it be trusted (is it in date, is the sample size good, is the gender split equal, is it their target market)? Bias: was it conducted fairly?
points: Worked example (Decreal Gear survey: Saturday 25th September 2021, 100 people, city centre, people aged 17–35 who exercise twice a week or more)
Saturday: good, people have more free time to answer. Date: not outdated (6 months before)
Sample of 100: not very reliable, too small to represent the whole market
City centre: busy on a Saturday, but for exercise a gym may be more appropriate
Valid: they asked their target market. But 52 male, 45 female, 3 other is imbalanced
Secondary research must be in date, appropriate to the business and from a reliable source (not Wikipedia)
Example: 2020 sportswear data was heavily affected by COVID lockdowns, so it may not reflect a lockdown-free world. Using unreliable data leads to poor decisions

sections.heading: Analysis tools: SWOT
sections.text: Analysis is examining information or data in detail to understand patterns, relationships, causes or implications. An analytical tool helps a business look at the market and the business as a whole, so it can decide which products to bring out or which area of the market to target. A SWOT analysis looks at the business itself (internal) and the external environment it could take advantage of.

head: What to look for
Examples
rows: Internal advantages, with evidence from the business model or market position
Brand image, product quality, unique design
Internal limitations; be honest but constructive, as areas to improve
Limited budget, small team, low brand awareness
External possibilities for growth, linked to the target audience or trends
Streetwear trends, social media marketing, influencer partnerships
External risks; show awareness of the wider market
Strong competition, changing consumer preferences, economic downturn

points: Exemplar SWOT for Decreal Gear: Strength: excellent reputation for quality (easier to get repeat custom). Weakness: sales revenue hasn't grown. Opportunity: sustainable materials could give a USP. Threat: lots of competitors could take market share
Make links to the scenario and write full sentences with clear explanations
Sentence starters: 'One of the key strengths is…', 'A current weakness that may affect the business is…', 'A growing trend the business could benefit from is…', 'Competitors pose a risk because…'
Use strengths and opportunities positively in the campaign, and plan how to reduce weaknesses and threats

sections.heading: Analysis tools: PESTLE
sections.text: PESTLE is another analytical tool. It assesses factors in the external environment that could affect the business, so it can make decisions and plan its campaign.

head: Factor
Examples from the slides
Impact on a business
rows: Tariffs add cost to imports/exports; after Brexit trade with the EU costs more and EU staff need visas; war can disrupt suppliers and flight paths
Exchange rates, interest rates, unemployment, cost of living
Exchange rates change import prices; higher interest makes a campaign loan cost more; high unemployment can mean a recession and low sales; high cost of living means less spending on luxuries
Impact of COVID, lifestyle (e.g. vegan), age distribution (ageing population), health consciousness
Adapt to new rules and changes; don't exclude a segment; meet the needs of different age groups
Automation, social media advertising, selling on a website
Faster production; reach a younger audience; sell 24/7
Legal: laws on advertising, consumers, employment
Wage rises increase costs; data must be protected with policies; faulty products must be refunded
Use recyclable packaging, cut waste and emissions; green credentials can improve brand image

points: Apply each factor to the case study and use precise examples, not vague statements
Explain how it could influence pricing, promotion, product development or distribution, using cause and effect: 'This could lead to…', 'As a result, the business may need to…'
Consider opportunities and threats, e.g. growing demand for sustainable products = opportunity; rising production costs = threat
Link back to the campaign: 'Based on this analysis, the business should focus on…' or 'The most influential factor is…'
Sentence frame: 'A [political] factor that could affect this business is… This could impact the business because… which would have the following impact… which could lead to…'

sections.heading: The 7 Ps marketing mix
sections.text: The marketing mix is made up of the 7 Ps: Product, Price, Place, Promotion, People, Process and Physical evidence (physical environment).
points: Strong exam answers link each P to the others and explain how it influences customer behaviour, fits the target market and supports the campaign

sections.heading: Product
sections.text: A product is anything that can be offered to a market to satisfy a want or need: physical goods, services, experiences, events, places, properties, organisations, information and ideas. It includes design, features, quality, branding and packaging.
points: Product differentiation is making a product different from others, to position it for different segments and gain an advantage over rivals, so customers can see their needs are met better
Ways to differentiate: unique and catchy names, quality, design/formulation/function, packaging, customer service
Form: the physical appearance, design and style (shape, colour, packaging, branding), e.g. an elegant perfume bottle appeals to high-end customers
Function: what the product does and how it meets needs, e.g. a smartwatch that tracks fitness and heart rate appeals to health-conscious and tech-savvy buyers

In the exam: find the product clues in the case study (features, design, branding, packaging, USPs), explain how it meets customer needs and stands out from competitors, and link it to price, promotion and place

sections.heading: The product life cycle
sections.text: The product life cycle (PLC) is the cycle every product goes through from introduction to withdrawal.

head: Stage
What happens
rows: Market research, prototypes, adverts released, product launched
If the launch works, sales increase sharply and the product may make a profit for the first time
Sales growth slows; repeat customers become loyal; the market becomes saturated as competitors bring out similar products
The product is outdated, sales fall, and eventually it is removed from sale

points: Extension strategies increase the life of a product by giving it fresh appeal or reaching a new segment: a new marketing campaign, a modified product, new packaging, anything that creates new interest
Example: what could Sony do to slow the decline of PlayStation 4 sales? Think of what they'd do at launch: new adverts, special editions, bundles, price cuts

diagram.alt: A product life cycle graph: sales (up the side) against time (along the bottom). Sales start low at introduction, rise steeply in growth, level off at maturity, then fall in decline. A dashed line from maturity shows an extension strategy (new campaign, modified product or new packaging) pushing sales back up.
diagram.caption: Extension strategies delay decline.

sections.heading: Price and pricing strategies
sections.text: Price is the amount a customer pays. The pricing strategy directly affects how customers see quality and value, the business's profit, and demand.

head: Strategy
How it works
rows: A low launch price (e.g. an introductory offer) to break into the market and win sales and market share; a short-term strategy, not always profitable
A high launch price when there is little competition, for high early returns; lowered later as rivals or newer models arrive (e.g. £349 down to £199)
Pricing in line with competitors so you don't seem to overcharge and lose market share
Add a profit margin to the unit cost, e.g. a TV costs £100 to make and sells for £200
High price to reflect quality; prices like £9.99 instead of £10

points: Price signals quality (99p vs £5.50 burger) and branding (£1.50 vs £30 t-shirt). Branded products usually cost more to make and promote
In competitive markets, price changes can have a big effect on demand
Influences on pricing: competition, market segment, PLC stage, costs (profit margin target), branding (strong brands charge more), technology (can lower costs)

sections.heading: Promotion
sections.text: Promotion is any marketing that aims to inform, persuade or motivate customers to buy or support a product. In a campaign it raises awareness, encourages trial or repeat purchases, builds brand loyalty and differentiates from competitors.

head: Method
What it is
Plus / minus
rows: A paid message aimed at influencing customers
Big impact in the right place / expensive, hard to measure
Managing reputation and goodwill by giving information
Builds trust and loyalty / slow to build, quickly damaged by bad publicity
Financially supporting events, people or organisations to raise awareness
Lots of exposure, links to a good cause / says little about the product
Face-to-face or phone selling by trained staff
Adverts on Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and similar
Low-cost, unconventional advertising in an unexpected place
Ideal for small businesses to make an impression
Paying for products to appear in TV or films
Raises awareness and shows the brand in use
Online channels using customer databases to target relevant promotions

points: Choose a strategy that fits the brand's values, target audience and budget; justify it against the business's goals and market; analyse short- and long-term benefits
Example: an e-commerce site reaches many customers, but if a business only delivers within 40 miles, wide reach could waste money

sections.heading: Place
sections.text: Place means making products available at the right place and the right time: in store or online.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Customers browse and try products; point-of-sale displays; staff give help and advice; many enjoy shopping
Running costs (rent, bills); limited opening hours; limited stock on display; higher prices
No expensive retail space; buy any time; reach customers worldwide; small firms can compete with large ones
Customers need internet access; can't pay cash; must wait for delivery; can't see items in person

points: Choosing a store location: cost, proximity to competitors, labour, resources and transport links
Direct distribution: manufacturer → customer (business to consumer or business to business)
Indirect distribution: through a third party, e.g. manufacturer → retailer → customer, or manufacturer → e-tailer → customer
Wholesalers buy in bulk from manufacturers and sell to smaller businesses such as retailers; retailers can be bricks-and-mortar or online
Most businesses use multiple distribution, e.g. their own website plus wholesalers

sections.heading: People, process and physical environment
points: People: the quality of employees who make, sell and service products, especially those dealing with customers. Better staff mean a better customer experience

Physical environment (physical evidence): where customers buy a product or experience it. Customers want to feel comfortable and find the information they need; it strongly affects purchases and repeat purchases
Process: customer service in buying and after-sales, handling complaints, finding customer needs, and the ordering process. A simpler process with fewer steps reduces abandoned sales

quiz.q: Which is one of the 4 key purposes of marketing?
quiz.e: Anticipate, recognise, stimulate and satisfy demand.

quiz.q: What is an aim?
o: A short-term target that is easy to change
The bigger picture: the main long-term thing a business wants to achieve
quiz.e: Objectives are the smaller, short-term steps that support it.

quiz.q: Which objective is SMART?
o: Improve customer satisfaction by 100% in 1 week
Increase sales revenue by 10% each month, for 12 months
quiz.e: It's specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and has a deadline.

quiz.q: What does the T in SMART stand for?
quiz.e: Objectives need a deadline, e.g. over 6 months.

quiz.q: What is a key characteristic of a niche market?
quiz.e: Niche marketing targets a small segment of a larger market, e.g. left-handed scissors.

quiz.q: Which best describes a mass market?
quiz.e: Mass marketing aims a product at all or most of the market, e.g. shampoo.

quiz.q: Grouping customers by lifestyle, values and interests is:
quiz.e: Demographic is age, gender, income; behavioural is how they use products.

quiz.q: Which is a method of market segmentation?
quiz.e: Geographic segmentation groups customers by where they are.

quiz.q: Amazon Prime's next-day delivery is an example of:
quiz.e: A USP separates a product from its competitors.

quiz.q: Which is an internal influence on a marketing campaign?
quiz.e: Internal: cost, finance, staff expertise, size and culture. The others are external.

quiz.q: Interviews and focus groups mainly produce:
quiz.e: They give in-depth opinions in words.

quiz.q: Which is secondary research?
quiz.e: Secondary research has already been collected by someone else.

quiz.q: A survey of only 100 people mainly affects the research's:
quiz.e: A small sample may not represent the whole market.

quiz.q: Why might 2020 sportswear data be unreliable?
o: COVID lockdowns changed how people shopped
It came from a trade journal
quiz.e: It may not reflect a lockdown-free world.

quiz.q: Which part of a SWOT analysis is external?
quiz.e: Opportunities and threats are external; strengths and weaknesses are internal.

quiz.q: Brexit and tariffs are which PESTLE factor?
quiz.e: Political factors come from government decisions.

quiz.q: A rise in the minimum wage is a … factor.
quiz.e: It's a law, and it increases business costs.

quiz.q: At which stage of the product life cycle does the market become saturated?
quiz.e: Competitors bring out similar products and sales growth slows.

quiz.q: A low launch price to win market share is:
quiz.e: Skimming is the opposite: a high launch price.

quiz.q: Paying for a product to appear in a film is:
quiz.e: It raises awareness by showing the brand in use.

quiz.q: Manufacturer → retailer → customer is:
quiz.e: It goes through a third party before the customer.

quiz.q: Which P is about how easy it is to order and the after-sales service?
quiz.e: A simpler process reduces abandoned sales.
